sections.title: 14. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Q&A

**Q1. Name the three types of drift and give one detection method for each.**
A: Data (input) drift = query distribution shifts; detect via PSI or embedding-distance histograms on inputs. Concept drift = input→correct-answer relationship shifts; detect via rolling accuracy on a labeled golden set. Prediction (output) drift = output distribution shifts; detect via PSI on output length, faithfulness, or judge-score distributions.

**Q2. Why is PSI often preferred over KL divergence for drift detection?**
A: PSI is symmetric (KL is not), bounded-ish in interpretation (<0.1 / 0.1–0.25 / >0.25 buckets), and stable on empty bins because of the epsilon-clip convention. KL diverges when a bin has zero count in either distribution. PSI also doesn't require distributional assumptions, which makes it usable on any binned metric.

**Q3. Why does p99 matter more for AI latency than p50?**
A: AI latency is heavy-tailed — long generations, multi-step agents, and tool calls can produce 10× median requests. A 200ms median improvement that hides a 30s p99 regression is a worse user experience, because users perceive "the bot froze" at the tail. p50 tracks efficiency; p99 tracks user-perceived reliability.

**Q4. What is alert fatigue and how do you prevent it?**
A: Alert fatigue is when on-call engineers start ignoring alerts because too many are non-actionable. Prevent by (a) requiring every alert to have a runbook, (b) routing non-urgent signals to Slack/dashboard instead of paging, (c) tuning thresholds against validated baselines, (d) reviewing alert volume monthly and demoting or deleting noisy alerts.

**Q5. Why is A/B testing AI harder than A/B testing traditional software?**
A: Three reasons: network effects (models share feedback data across arms, breaking independence), long-tail tasks (quality is dominated by the 20% tail, requiring huge sample sizes for power), and non-stationarity (user behavior shifts mid-experiment). Interleaved testing and pre-experiment power calculations mitigate these.

**Q6. How do you do reference-free quality evaluation in production?**
A: You can't compute exact-match without ground truth, so use reference-free metrics: faithfulness (is the answer supported by retrieved context?), groundedness, internal consistency, and LLM-judge rubrics. Sample 1–5% of traffic, score offline, and track the distribution with drift tests.

**Q7. What's the bias problem with user feedback, and how do you mitigate it?**
A: Happy users don't rate; ratings skew toward extreme experiences. Mitigate by weighting implicit signals (regenerate, copy, dwell) more heavily than explicit thumbs, using explicit feedback for outlier detection rather than averaging, and segmenting feedback by user cohort to surface silent churn.

**Q8. How often should you refresh your golden/eval dataset?**
A: Continuously. Production-sampled, human-triaged examples should flow into the golden set weekly. Stale golden sets can't detect new failure modes; an eval suite frozen at launch is blind to drift by construction.

**Q9. What's the difference between an SLI and an SLO, and give an AI example.**
A: SLI is the measurement; SLO is the target. Example: SLI = rolling 24h faithfulness on sampled production traffic; SLO = faithfulness ≥ 0.85 for 99% of rolling 24h windows. Breaching the SLO consumes error budget; exhausting the budget triggers a feature freeze.

**Q10. Why is cost-per-task-success better than cost-per-request?**
A: Cost-per-request optimizes toward cheap, dumb models. Cost-per-task-success ties spend to outcome — a model that costs 2× per request but succeeds 3× more often is cheaper per successful outcome, which is what the business actually pays for.

### B. Scenario-Based Questions

**Scenario**: Faithfulness on your RAG chatbot dropped from 0.92 to 0.85 over a week. No code change, no model change. Your ops metrics are flat. Debug.
**Task**: Propose a debugging plan and likely root causes.
**Sample Answer**: Start by ruling out the obvious: confirm no silent model provider change by checking the model-version header on traces. Then check retrieval quality — faithfulness drops in RAG are usually retrieval regressions, not generation regressions. Look at PSI on retrieved-chunk relevance scores and on query embeddings to detect query drift. Inspect the index: was it rebuilt, swapped, or polluted? Check for embedding-model version drift if you use a hosted embedder. Pull the lowest-faithfulness traces from the week and look for patterns — same source documents? same query type? If retrieval is fine, the model may have undergone a silent provider-side update; compare outputs on a frozen golden set against pre-drop snapshots. Most weeks the answer is "retrieval index got corrupted or rebuilt with stale data."

**Scenario**: Your daily LLM cost doubled overnight. Traffic is unchanged. Investigate.
**Task**: Where do you look, and what's the most likely cause?
**Sample Answer**: First, break cost down by model and by request. If the model mix shifted (more traffic routed to the expensive model), it's a router bug — check the router logs and the routing-rule diff. If the mix is the same but per-request cost doubled, the average prompt length grew; check the prompt token distribution, look at the top-5 expensive requests, and inspect their traces for pathological retrieval (e.g., 20k-token contexts). Look for a single user or session burning disproportionate budget — a feedback loop where the model keeps retrying or the user keeps regenerating. Also check whether prompt caching broke: a sudden drop in cache hit rate doubles effective input cost with no traffic change. Most often this is either a router regression, a retrieval bug bloating context, or a cache invalidation.

**Scenario**: Users report the bot is "worse" but your dashboards look fine — latency, error rate, faithfulness, judge score all green. Why?
**Task**: Explain what your metrics might be missing.
**Sample Answer**: Your metrics are probably averaging over the wrong population. Three likely culprits. First, sampling bias: if your eval samples only "successful" requests (e.g., requests that returned without a safety refusal), you're not measuring the failures users experience. Second, long-tail blindness: aggregate faithfulness can hold steady while the worst 5% of queries gets dramatically worse — track p5 faithfulness, not just mean. Third, metric blind spots: faithfulness measures "is the answer supported by retrieved context" but doesn't measure tone, completeness, or helpfulness — a confidently-cited-but-incomplete answer scores well on faithfulness and fails users. Pull the actual user complaints, find their traces, and check whether your metrics would have caught them. If not, you have a metric design gap, not a system regression.

**Scenario**: Your boss wants to ship a model update tomorrow. p99 latency in staging is 12 seconds, up from 4 seconds. They say "users won't notice, it's an internal tool." What do you say?
**Task**: Respond with a clear position and supporting reasoning.
**Sample Answer**: Don't ship as-is. p99 of 12 seconds means 1 in 100 requests freezes for over 12 seconds — long enough that users will assume the system is broken, refresh, and either retry (doubling load) or escalate. Even for internal tools, perceived latency is a trust signal; users who lose trust in the bot stop using it, and the project dies from disuse. Propose three options in order: (a) investigate the regression — p99 jumps are usually a specific pathological path (long generation, tool timeout, retry loop) that can be fixed without rolling back the model; (b) ship behind a feature flag with a hard p99 SLO and auto-rollback if staging p99 exceeds 6s; (c) ship to a 5% canary first with p99 monitoring for 48h. The right answer is almost always (a) — find the pathological path, fix it, then ship.

**Scenario**: You're asked to set up monitoring for a brand-new AI feature that launches in two weeks. What do you instrument on day one?
**Task**: List the must-have signals and why.
**Sample Answer**: On day one, capture three things. First, traces — every request must produce a trace tree with span attributes (model, prompt version, retrieved chunks, token counts, cost, latency, status). Without traces, post-hoc debugging is impossible. Second, baseline distributions — log faithfulness, latency, cost, and query-embedding distributions for the first week of staging traffic; these baselines are the reference for all future drift detection. Third, a feedback channel — even a simple thumbs-down button, plus implicit signals (regenerate, copy). Skip the fancy LLM-judge pipeline for week one; you don't have enough traffic to make it statistically meaningful. Add the judge in week three once you have a baseline to compare against. The unifying principle: you cannot detect drift, alert on regressions, or build a golden set later if you didn't capture the right signals on day one.
